Stage 3 · Grammar

Criticizing something that is already done

Two forms, and the whole of English regret runs through them.

Read these two sentences.
  • She should have been more careful when she posted the video.
  • She shouldn’t have accepted her boss as a ‘friend’ online.
What do these two sentences tell you about what she actually did?
This structure does not imagine an alternative. It passes judgement.

Should have and shouldn’t have look back at something that was actually done, or actually not done, and say it was wrong. That makes them more direct than the third conditional you met in the previous lesson. If I hadn’t posted it, I’d still have my job imagines a different past; I shouldn’t have posted it convicts.

The two forms divide the ground cleanly. Should have + past participle criticises an omission: the right thing was not done. She should have been more careful when she posted the video. Shouldn’t have + past participle criticises an action: the wrong thing was done. He shouldn’t have said anything negative about the interviewer online.

A third option sits alongside them and is often the more useful one socially. Could have points out an alternative that existed, without assigning blame. You could have told me notes a missed option; You should have told me says you were wrong not to. When you are talking to a colleague or a friend rather than analysing your own mistake, could have is frequently the better choice.

Structurally there is one thing to fix and it applies to every modal in the perfect: the modal never changes. The pastness is carried entirely by have + past participle. That is why should had does not exist, and why should’ve — which sounds exactly like should of — is always written should have.

Before you look at the table: the table below separates criticism of an action from criticism of an omission, and adds the softer could have. Decide which column you are in before you choose the form.
The form — and the meaning it carries
FormExampleWhat actually happened
should have + participleHe should have thought before pressing Send.He didn’t think.
shouldn’t have + participleShe shouldn’t have posted the video.She did post it.
should never haveI should never have clicked Send.Stronger regret.
could have + participleYou could have waited until the morning.A softer criticism — the option existed.
QuestionShould I have said something?Asking for a verdict.
Related regretIf only I hadn’t pressed Send. Lesson 31Same meaning, different structure.

The form never changes. should have + past participle, for everybody: I should have, she should have, they should have. There is no -s and no to.

Should have means it did not happen; shouldn’t have means it did. This is the opposite of what learners expect, and it is worth saying out loud twice.

The mistake to avoid. Not should have went but should have gone. The participle, not the past simple. Same with seen, done, written, taken.

Could have is the kind version. To a real person, You could have called me lands very differently from You should have called me — the first names an option, the second names a failure. Choose deliberately.

Full grammar reference — should have and shouldn’t have — criticising past actions

What it is

Should have + past participle says that the right thing was not done. Shouldn’t have + past participle says that the wrong thing was done. Both look back at a completed action and judge it. The form of the modal never changes; the past meaning is carried entirely by have + past participle.

What it means, and what it does

This structure is how English expresses regret about your own behaviour and criticism of somebody else’s. It is more direct than the third conditional: If I hadn’t posted it… imagines an alternative, but I shouldn’t have posted it passes judgement. That is why it dominates apologies, post-mortems and any conversation about a decision that went wrong.

When and why we use it

Should have and shouldn’t have look back at something that was actually done, or actually not done, and say it was wrong. That makes them more direct than the third conditional you met in the previous lesson. If I hadn’t posted it, I’d still have my job imagines a different past; I shouldn’t have posted it convicts.

The two forms divide the ground cleanly. Should have + past participle criticises an omission: the right thing was not done. She should have been more careful when she posted the video. Shouldn’t have + past participle criticises an action: the wrong thing was done. He shouldn’t have said anything negative about the interviewer online.

A third option sits alongside them and is often the more useful one socially. Could have points out an alternative that existed, without assigning blame. You could have told me notes a missed option; You should have told me says you were wrong not to. When you are talking to a colleague or a friend rather than analysing your own mistake, could have is frequently the better choice.

Structurally there is one thing to fix and it applies to every modal in the perfect: the modal never changes. The pastness is carried entirely by have + past participle. That is why should had does not exist, and why should’ve — which sounds exactly like should of — is always written should have.

Typical situations

You need this for apologising and accepting responsibility, for reviewing a decision that went badly at work, for criticising or defending somebody else’s behaviour, and for talking about anything you regret.

  • Regretting something you did — shouldn’t have.I shouldn’t have said anything negative about the interviewer online.
  • Regretting something you failed to do — should have.She should have been more careful when she posted the video.
  • Criticising another person — the same forms, aimed outward.They should have given him the job anyway, if he was the best candidate.
  • Suggesting a missed alternative — could have — softer, no blame attached.He could have waited until the offer arrived.
  • Expressing relief in hindsight — the negative of an unwanted outcome.I shouldn’t have worried — nobody noticed.
  • Apologising — the structure inside an apology.I’m really sorry — I should never have sent it.

How it differs from similar structures

should have = it was the right thing and you did not do it · shouldn’t have = it was the wrong thing and you did it · could have = it was an available option, without blame.
should have + past participle = criticism of a real past action · would have + past participle = the imagined result of an unreal condition (Lesson 31). He should have waited vs He would have got the job.

How to build it

Criticism of an omission: subject + should have + past participle
Criticism of an action: subject + shouldn’t have + past participle
Softer, no blame: subject + could have + past participle
Emphatic: subject + should never have + past participle
AffirmativeHe should have thought before pressing Send.
NegativeShe shouldn’t have accepted her boss as a friend online.
Emphatic negativeI should never have uploaded it.
QuestionShould he have told his boss the truth?
PassiveThe photo shouldn’t have been posted at all.
ContinuousShe shouldn’t have been filming at the party.
Short answerYes, he should have. / No, she shouldn’t have.
Contracted speechshould’ve /ˈʃʊdəv/ · shouldn’t’ve /ˈʃʊdntəv/

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • should have reduces to should’ve /ˈʃʊdəv/, which sounds almost identical to should of. It is always have; should of is never correct in writing.
  • In the negative, the l is silent and the d is often swallowed: shouldn’t’ve comes out as /ˈʃʊnəv/ in fast speech.
  • Stress on should marks the criticism: You SHOULD have told me.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The modal never changes form. The pastness lives in have + past participle. Should have is the past of should, in the same way that must have been is the past of must be (Lesson 26).
  • Could have is not the same as should have. You could have told me points out a missed option; You should have told me says you were wrong not to. Could have is far less confrontational.
  • Must have is deduction, not criticism: He must have forgotten is a conclusion about what happened, not a judgement about what ought to have happened.
  • Should have is close in meaning to ought to have, which is slightly more formal and much less common in speech.
  • The structure often pairs with the third conditional in the same turn: I shouldn’t have posted it. If I hadn’t, I’d still have the job. The first judges, the second imagines.
  • In an apology, should never have is stronger than shouldn’t have and signals that you accept full responsibility.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I should of checked the video first. → I should have checked the video first.Should’ve is should have, never of.
  • She should had been more careful. → She should have been more careful.Modals are followed by have, never had.
  • He shouldn’t have posted anything negative, if he didn’t, he’d have the job. → He shouldn’t have posted anything negative. If he hadn’t, he’d have the job.Keep the criticism and the third conditional as separate sentences.
  • I should have to tell my boss the truth. → I should have told my boss the truth.Should takes no to, and the past needs the participle.
  • She shouldn’t have accepted him as friend. → She shouldn’t have accepted him as a friend.A singular countable noun needs an article.
  • You must have told me earlier. → You should have told me earlier.Must have is deduction; criticism takes should have.

More examples in context

  • self-criticismI shouldn’t have tweeted about the interview.
  • omissionHe should have waited until he was offered the job.
  • criticising othersThey should have given him the job anyway, if he was the best candidate.
  • softer alternativeShe could have checked the privacy settings first.
  • emphatic regretI should never have told my boss I was ill.
  • passiveThe video shouldn’t have been uploaded at all.
  • continuousHe shouldn’t have been tweeting from the stadium.
  • questionShould his friend have asked before writing about the party online?
  • in an apologyI’m really sorry — I should have thought before I pressed send.
  • paired with a conditionalI shouldn’t have posted it. If I hadn’t, I would still have my job.

A tip for remembering it

Two questions decide the form. Did you do it? If yes and it was wrong → shouldn’t have. If no and it was right → should have. Then check the spelling of the second word: it is always have, never of and never had. Say should’ve aloud and write should have.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Should have + past participle = you didn’t do the right thing.
  2. Shouldn’t have + past participle = you did the wrong thing.
  3. The modal never changes; have + past participle carries the past.
  4. Could have points out a missed option without blaming.
  5. Must have is a deduction, not a criticism.
  6. Write should have, never should of or should had.

9a · Read the whole text first. Then choose the form that fits each gap.

More than a quarter of social-media users send messages they later regret. The pattern is always the same. Somebody reads something that upsets them, replies within a minute, and by the morning is thinking: I written that. Researchers say the real mistake happens earlier: people at all while they are still angry. One manager described uploading a video to the company account by accident. ‘I which account I was logged into,’ she said. ‘And I deleted it in the first minute, but I panicked.’ Her colleagues it within seconds. The advice from every study is the same, and it is dull: if you the urge to reply immediately, wait an hour. Almost nobody has ever thought, an hour later, that they the angry version.
